title: Joseph Calasanz (25 August)
hookLine: he opened the first free public school in Europe (1597)
tomorrow: The death of John the Baptist (29 August)

cards: Joseph Calasanz came to Rome, the story goes, hoping for a good church post. A priest from Spain, with plans. Then he started noticing the children in the poor streets: running loose, working, getting into trouble.
None of them in school, because school cost money and their families had none. He asked the parish to teach them. No room.
He asked others. Nobody took it on. So he did it himself: he found rooms, gathered the children, and taught them reading, writing, sums and the faith, and charged nothing.
The good church post never mattered again.

teach.b: He called them the Pious Schools, and the order he founded to run them is known as the Piarists. The idea was simple and, for its time, bold: a poor child's mind is worth teaching, properly, and for free.
Not charity on the side. Real lessons, every day, alongside prayer.
Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "he that shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me." Calasanz took that literally. Every child at the door was a guest of that kind.
The schools grew, and other teachers joined.
Then, near the end of his life, the story turns hard. Men inside his own order worked against him. He was removed from leading it, and the order itself was cut down and stripped of its standing.
Everything he had built looked finished. Tradition remembers that he didn't fight it with bitterness. He kept praying, kept obeying, kept teaching where he could, and forgave the men who had done it.
He died with the work in ruins.
After his death, the order was restored, and the schools went on.
The Church later named him a patron of Christian schools. So the lesson has two halves. Everyone deserves an education, including the child whose family can't pay.
And when the good thing you built is taken from you, Calasanz's answer, in the story, was patience, and it outlived the men who opposed him.

how: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph Calasanz on 25 August; Piarist schools and parishes honor him as their founder, and Catholic teachers ask his prayers for their students.

games.q: you came to Rome hoping for a good church post. poor children run the streets with no school, and the parish says there's no room. what do you do?
o: keep after your post. the children aren't your job.
find rooms and teach them yourself, for free.
teach them, but charge a small fee to keep it going.
games.why: the story goes that he found rooms and taught them himself, for nothing. the good church post never mattered again.

practice: Calasanz started with what he had: reading, writing, sums.
Pick one thing you could teach, a skill your hands know, a language, how to cook one good meal, and picture someone who might need it: the two of you, and the thing passing between you.
If you pray, ask Saint Joseph Calasanz to pray for the children learning right now with very little; if not, hold them in mind with hope.
